articles.title: Trump awards ‘America’s Mayor’ Giuliani nation’s highest civilian honor
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday presented former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. Giuliani was heralded for his actions after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York, becoming known as “America’s Mayor.” A White House official called him “one of the greatest leaders in…
articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday presented former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom , the nation’s highest civilian honor.

Giuliani was heralded for his actions after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York, becoming known as “America’s Mayor.” A White House official called him “one of the greatest leaders in New York City history who has dedicated his life to serving others.”

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales described Giuliani as “a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“President Trump will proudly honor Mayor Giuliani — America’s Mayor — with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his lifetime of service to the American people,” Wales said in a statement.

Giuliani said he is “honored and humbled” to receive the award .

“Any and all distinction I have received in public office is fully the result of following the advice of my boss, Ronald Reagan, who said: ‘There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit,’” he said in a statement.

“I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,” the Trump ally added.

Andrew Giuliani, the former mayor’s son, said the ceremony was “beautiful.”

“There’s been nobody more consequential in the history of New York City,” he told reporters at the White House. “And certainly, nobody that saved more lives than Rudy Guiliani.”

Giuliani’s tenure as mayor was also known for his prosecution of several New York City crime bosses and other “tough on crime” policies.

He ran a brief campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008 but ultimately dropped out and endorsed the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.).

Giuliani and Trump have known each other for decades, with the former mayor becoming a big backer of the president’s first White House bid in 2016. He later joined Trump’s legal team and led the efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

He faced two defamation cases in connection to unsubstantiated election fraud claims. He also faced charges in Georgia under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act.

He was disbarred in New York and Washington for repeatedly making false statements about the election.

Trump said last year he would be awarding Giuliani the medal after the former mayor suffered serious injuries in a car accident.

“As President of the United States of America, I am pleased to announce that Rudy Giuliani, the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot, will receive THE PRESIDENTIAL MEDAL OF FREEDOM, our Country’s highest civilian honor,” he wrote on Truth Social last September.

The president pardoned Giuliani and other allies connected to the efforts to overturn the 2020 election in November 2025.

During his second term, Trump has awarded the medal posthumously to Welles Crowther, an equities trader and volunteer firefighter who died while helping to save lives on 9/11, and to conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated in September 2025.

During his first term he also awarded the honor to several people, including posthumously to famed baseball player Babe Ruth and Elvis Presley. Others included golf legend Tiger Woods and conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh.

articles.title: Biden's first-year fundraising fails to crack 1% of Obama's library haul as questions swirl over legacy
articles.summary: Joe Biden raised just $1.5 million for his presidential library in 2025, per tax filings, a fraction of the $232.6 million Barack Obama brought in 2017.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden has raised a shockingly small amount of funds for his presidential library compared to former President Barack Obama. The figures are fueling skepticism about how history will remember Biden's single term in the White House. In 2017, Obama’s first year out of office, the two-term president managed to bring in $232.6 million in donations and contributions to fund the foundation behind his presidential library. By comparison, Biden secured just $1.5 million in 2025 for his presidential library foundation, per tax filings. This is less than 1% of what his former boss raised in the same amount of time after leaving office. Even before leaving office, President Donald Trump’s library foundation has already dwarfed that of his predecessor by raising tens of millions of dollars from a variety of sources, including companies that settled lawsuits with him. OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER. Though the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation has yet to decide on a construction site, it’s already running a deficit, spending $600,000 more than it raised in 2025. A Biden library official claimed that it wasn’t actively fundraising in 2025 in a statement shared with CBS News. The lack of enthusiasm for Biden’s legacy has led some to claim that Americans may simply forget about his presidency as the years go on. "Presidencies usually fade," Axios’ Zachary Basu wrote of his legacy. "But in just one year, Biden’s has been reduced to a footnote by a successor committed to dismantling every pillar of Washington’s old liberal order." Heritage Action press manager Doug Blair told Fox News Digital, "Joe Biden spent half a century in Washington and did nothing to benefit the American people." "The anemic fundraising for his presidential library is a fitting bookend for a failed presidency Americans are eager to forget," he added. "Joe Biden left Americans worse off by every conceivable measure and his legacy will be a southern border blown wide open, the disgraceful image of him checking his watch as fallen American troops returned home from Afghanistan, and endless scandals and investigations surrounding him and his corrupt family.' BIDEN'S BATTLE WITH ADVANCING CANCER RENEWS FOCUS ON PROSTATE DISEASE Allies of the former president point to the fact that Biden presided over the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, influential pieces of domestic legislation and America’s withdrawal from Afghanistan, parts of his legacy that could contribute to historical staying power. A January 2025 Gallup poll found that 54% of U.S. adults believed history would remember Biden as a "below-average" or "poor" president. A source close to Biden’s foundation told CBS News that it ramped up its fundraising in 2026, pulling in multiple multi-million-dollar contributions, including two $5 million donations. Another source told the outlet that some of Biden's close allies are frustrated that Democratic donors aren’t stepping up to support the former president’s library. Further complicating Biden’s fundraising efforts, and his ability to nurture his public image, is his advanced age and Stage 4 prostate cancer, which has metastasized to his bones. OBAMA CENTER OPENS AFTER YEARS-LONG SAGA AS LOCALS WARN ‘MONSTROSITY’ COULD PRICE THEM OUT While the increase in funds is no doubt encouraging for Biden’s allies, it still puts them far behind Obama, who raised $164.8 million for his foundation in 2018. Obama ultimately spent nearly $1 billion on his presidential library in Chicago, a sum Biden likely will not be able to reach given his current fundraising levels. articles.title: Time for new leadership in Senate
articles.summary: The article argues that Sen. Chuck Schumer should step down as Senate Democratic leader in favor of Sen. Chris Van Hollen to reflect the generational and policy changes demanded by voters following the November election.
articles.body:
It was tense, it was tough, but it was necessary. On July 13, 2024, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) drove four hours from his home in Brooklyn to President Joe Biden’s beach house in Rehoboth Beach, Del. His mission: To tell the president that, for the good of the country and the Democratic Party, he should drop out of the campaign and not run for reelection.

Now is the time for Schumer to take his own advice.

And now is the time for Senate Democrats to elect Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) as their new leader.

That sounds harsh, coming so soon after Democrats — thanks in great part to Schumer’s leadership — swept to a stunning nine-seat majority in the Senate. It was also harsh for Biden, having saved the country from President Trump in 2020. But the times demanded a change in leadership then, and they demand a change in leadership now.

Can Schumer take credit for Democrats’ winning 56 seats in the Senate? Absolutely. He recruited or strongly supported eight out of nine candidates who ended up flipping Republican seats: Sherrod Brown in Ohio; Roy Cooper in North Carolina; Adam Hamilton in Kansas; Mary Peltola in Alaska; Annie Andrews in South Carolina; James Tallarico in Texas; Josh Turek in Iowa; and Scott Colom in Mississippi.

It wasn’t a perfect record. Schumer made a big mistake in Maine, initially supporting Gov. Janet Mills (D), and put Michigan in jeopardy by supporting Rep. Haley Stevens (D) in the primary . Had he put more resources behind Angie Nixon (D) in Florida and Jamie Davis (D) in Louisiana , Democrats might have wound up flipping 11 seats, and not just nine. But still, it’s hard to argue with Schumer’s success.

So, yes indeed, give Schumer all the thanks and credit he’s due for engineering Democrats’ phenomenally successful efforts to regain control of the Senate. But that should not in itself propel him automatically into a continued role as Democratic leader. In fact, by retaining Schumer in that post, Democrats would ignore the clear message sent by voters on Nov. 3.

Given the historic margins by which Democrats won in the House and the Senate, there’s no doubt that, more than anything else, Americans want change — leadership change, generational change and policy change. Keeping Schumer in place provides none of the three.

As several senators and senators-elect supporting Van Hollen have stated, responding to the kind of change voters demanded on Nov. 3 first requires a new face at the top. “I think the American public spoke loud and clear about what they wanted to see in the country and from this new generation of leadership,” [“I hink the American public spoke loud and clear about what they wanted to see in the country and from this new generation of leadership,” said Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) in endorsing Van Hollen. “Not marginal change, not small nibbling at the edges.”

You can’t pretend to field a new team with the same, old, tired coach who’s been Senate Democratic leader for almost ten years.

Judging by the historic turnout of young people and the young candidates they elected, voters want younger leaders, as well. True, at 67, Van Hollen’s not that young, but he’s clearly more in touch with millennials than the 76-year-old Schumer, who last year refused to endorse Zohran Mamdani , the young, Democratic candidate for mayor of his hometown, New York City. Unlike Schumer, Van Hollen also shares with younger voters a growing disaffection with the hardline policies of the Israeli government under Benjamin Netanyahu and a willingness to cut back on unlimited military support for the Israeli military.

Most importantly, perhaps, to seize the moment, benefit from their success on Nov. 3, and prepare to expand those gains in 2028, Democrats need a strong messenger. And be honest, stooped over and looking so old, with his glasses perched on the end of his nose, Chuck Schumer just doesn’t fit the bill.

On every level, Van Hollen is a stronger choice as leader. Is that fair for Schumer, who has served in public office for the last 51 years? Maybe not. But who says politics is fair? Politics is about getting things done. And politics is also about knowing when to step down and pass the torch.

Schumer ended his July 2024 meeting with Biden by advising the president , “If I had to leave politics tomorrow for whatever reason, I would say to myself, ‘All the s— we take in this job was worth it for making the world a better place.’”

Schumer has also helped make the world a better place. Thank you, Chuck — but now is the time to go.

It’s Tuesday. Two days out from Thanksgiving… close but not close enough.

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com .

The U.S. Army appears determined to go through with the lead azide detonations in Iowa on Wednesday after multiple postponements due to resident and lawmaker blowback.

“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first,” said acting Army Secretary Adam Telle in a post to the social platform X.

Telle said during a press conference on Tuesday the munitions will take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown at 10 a.m. EST on Wednesday.

The explosion will set off a plume of lead-containing particles into the air, which has sparked alarm from local officials.

Officials fire back : Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D), Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D) and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) have all fired back on the Army’s handling of the planned detonation, sighting environmental concerns and disruptions for residents.

“This is a total failure and Iowans deserve better,” Hinson said on Monday. “There must be a thorough investigation with real accountability to ensure this never happens again in Iowa or anywhere else in the country.”

Buck stops where? President Trump said he would not move forward with the Army’s plan unless Sand and the courts give permission. Sand responded by effectively saying it was on federal officials to handle the problem and explain their decision.

A three-judge panel for the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined Monday to halt the detonation, denying an emergency request from environmental groups.

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) backed the detonation on Tuesday, writing, “I believe, based on the information I’ve been given, that the danger is immediate, and I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected.”

It is one day after the Nvidia board of directors announced Jensen Huang returned as CEO, and negative reactions continue to pour out from lawmakers and other figures on the right.

Political commentator Bill O’Reilly appeared on NewsNation’s “On Balance” and said Huang should have been suspended and investigated for a “variety of crimes, including harming the nation.”

“To say that he, Huang, is innocent, just gives Bernie Sanders more power,” O’Reilly said, adding “the president in defending Huang, on saying that he didn’t do anything wrong, allows the opposition to run wild.”

Trump said Monday that he “convinced” the Nvidia board to reinstate the Nvidia CEO, saying, “I spoke to them, let me put it that way.”

Fox News host Jesse Watters also said Trump’s defense would give Democrats “ammunition” to go after the president.

“The Democrats are now licking their chops over the Jensen affair and Trump personally restoring him as CEO, even if it was to help the economy and the country,” Watters said.

“The Democrats will likely use this scandal to impeach,” he added.

The Committees agree: Republican chairs of three House committees — Brian Mast (Fla.) on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar (Mich.) on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and Rick Crawford (Ark.) on the House Intelligence Committee — wrote a joint statement speaking out.

“The NVIDIA board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” they wrote.

Huang is set to provide testimony to House lawmakers in a closed door hearing on Dec. 1, before appearing for a public hearing of the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3 at 10:00 a.m. EST.

The U.S. Army announced on Monday that it is looking to resume helicopter training flights out of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport nearly two years after the deadly midair collision that killed 67 people.

Rep. Don Byer (D-Va.), whose district holds the airport, said on Monday that Army officials had contacted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on resuming the flights.

“The path forward must prioritize safety, and that requires full implementation of the NTSB’s recommendations before training flights resume,” Byer wrote on the social platform X.

Safety concerns mount: The request to resume flights comes with controversy, after training helicopters were banned around Reagan National Airport a little less than two years ago.

On Jan. 29, 2025, an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Airlines regional passenger jet in, killing everyone aboard both aircrafts.

In May 2025, all training helicopter flights were banned after another Black Hawk had a close call with a passenger plane.

Signed, (un)sealed, delivered, they’re (partially) yours: A federal court on Monday unsealed heavily redacted documents related to the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home in Washington, D.C., last month.

Federal prosecutors had made a last-minute push to block the release of the files.

The nearly 170 pages of records reveal a little bit of information regarding the scope of the investigation — federal investigators sought evidence of potential criminal violations from Omar dating back to 1980.

Some background: The 44-year-old immigrated to the U.S. from Somalia in 1995 and became a naturalized citizen in 2000.

Federal authorities are reportedly investigating whether Omar or her relatives provided false information on her paperwork. She has denied the allegations.

“The United States believes ILHAN has committed [redacted] crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” prosecutors wrote in one filing.

Who wants ’em?: A coalition of 14 news organizations — including The Associated Press, The Washington Post and CNN — petitioned the court for access to the records.

Prosecutors opposed and argued it could jeopardize the investigation.

Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg agreed with the Justice Department that the bulk of the records from the Oct. 12 raid should remain sealed, including a 67-page affidavit detailing the basis of the search.

Boasberg ordered the disclosure of portions of the records that did not identify witnesses or divulge potential criminal charges.

Actors Jane Fonda and Robert De Niro joined dozens of celebrities and Democratic donors in endorsing Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to become Senate majority leader.

In a letter released Tuesday, 35 celebrities and political donors argued that keeping Schumer, who is currently the Senate minority leader, in power would run counter to voters’ demands for change that fueled Democrats’ resounding victories in the midterm elections, The New York Times reported .

The signatories, who said they contributed or helped raise about $23 million for Democratic congressional candidates this cycle, also include comedian Chelsea Handler, actor Marisa Tomei, television personality Padma Lakshmi and former BlackRock executive Morris Pearl, according to the Times.

The group urged Democratic senators to publicly disclose whom they intend to support in the Dec. 1 leadership election.

“The Senate Democratic leader will be chosen behind closed doors, by secret ballot,” the letter reads. “No senator will ever have to tell voters, or us, how they voted. We believe a decision this consequential deserves public accountability.”

The group, which includes signatories that have previously donated to Schumer, expressed frustration with the New York Democrat’s limited support for progressive Senate candidates this cycle, including Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) and Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), who lost her Senate bid.

“Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty and policies of [President] Trump and his [Jeffrey] Epstein-class cronies,” De Niro said in a statement to the Times. “That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership.”

Handler pointed to Van Hollen’s trip to El Salvador last year to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident who was mistakenly deported by the Trump administration.

“This is an opportunity. This is a window,” Handler told the outlet. “We need to, like, get the ball and run with it. And I don’t believe that Chuck Schumer is going to do that.”

Van Hollen has sought to make the leadership contest a referendum on how Democrats should wield their newfound majority. The party, which will control 56 seats in January, picked up nine Senate seats in the midterms, including in deep-red states such as Texas and Kansas.

articles.title: Congress must not chicken out on investigating Nvidia
articles.summary: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO following pressure from President Trump, prompting calls for Congress to exercise its oversight authority regarding potential national security risks and chip exports to China.
articles.body:
For the last two years, I have described Washington with the acronym CACO, or Congress Always Chickens Out. Now comes the first real test since voters overwhelmingly demanded change earlier this month. Jensen Huang has been abruptly reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive despite serious national security concerns, and Congress has to decide what to do about it. It can use its Article I powers to find out what happened, or it can chicken out again.

Less than two weeks after Huang resigned over an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese asset (plus alleged affairs with two Nvidia executives ), Nvidia’s board brought him back on Monday, citing “ input from senior levels of the United States government .” That input came from the president. In an interview Monday, President Trump boasted that the board would not have changed its mind without him, and said that he personally talked its members into it. When he was asked about the woman’s contacts with China’s Ministry of State Security, he brushed the question aside.

According to the New York Times , U.S. intelligence tracked her contacts with an officer of the Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until this fall. Her business partner also worked with the agency, and her company is suspected of supplying Nvidia chips to contractors for China’s military. Within days, and after Nvidia’s stock price dropped precipitously, the administration put those concerns aside and vouched for Huang to his board. When a White House overrules its own intelligence professionals that quickly, and won’t explain why, it severely undermines trust in the intelligence community.

If, as the president says, a thorough investigation cleared Huang, the administration should let Congress see it. So far, it has shared little of the intelligence with Capitol Hill, and last week it postponed a briefing for senior national security staff. Who gave the board its assurances, and what were they based on? Those questions are all the more pressing after House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.) revealed that the administration had approved export licenses covering more than 879,000 advanced Nvidia and AMD chips for China , including for companies the Pentagon designates as Chinese military companies. And at the end of last year, the president owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock .

Any administration should not be in a position to investigate itself, which is why Americans are looking to Congress. They made their frustrations clear on Election Day. Republicans and Democrats should work together to get to the bottom of this and show they heard those voters.

Some of that work has begun, with Huang due to sit for closed-door interviews with three House committees on Dec. 1 and to testify at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3 . That’s a start, but Congress should be bold. Put witnesses under oath and ask them tough questions. Bring in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, along with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche, whom the president says he consulted before vouching for Huang. And if the facts call for action, such as tighter export controls on our most advanced chips, pass them.

It may be tempting to wait until Democrats take over in January, but Republicans have a chance to show some independence from an administration that voters just rejected. If Congress means to use its Article I powers, now is the time.

Nvidia is not the only urgent test in front of this lame duck Congress, which should also restore the Russia sanctions it passed in September, after the president waived them a month later, and keep the government open past Dec. 11.

The question now is whether Congress will finally assert its authority or chicken out one more time.

Jane Harman represented California’s 36th District in Congress for nine terms and served as ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

The birds, hailing from a West Virginia farm, were given patriotic names in honor of America’s 250th birthday . They will retire to Texas A&M University after receiving their clemency.

articles.body:
Conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt said Republicans should match the Democrats’ debate scheduling for the 2028 presidential election primaries.

“The DNC [Democratic National Committee] announced its plan for 5 presidential primary debates in 2027 beginning in June/July and 7 in 2028,” Hewitt said Monday evening on the social platform X .

“President Trump should strongly recommend the RNC [Republican National Committee] at least mirror the DNC schedule or he and the GOP will be battered without the ability to respond for months,” he added.

The DNC announced Monday it is planning 12 presidential primary debates for the 2028 cycle, with the first set for June 2027.

In a Monday press release obtained by The Hill’s partner network NewsNation, the DNC said five of the debates will happen in 2027, with the other seven set for the election year. The debates will kick off next June, with another debate the following month and the final debate happening in March 2028, per the DNC.

“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said in a statement.

“The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House,” he added.

The DNC also said that it will unveil locations and media partners for the first two debates in January.

Democrats are fresh off their expansive midterm wins, in which they took back the House and Senate and delivered a blow to Trump and the GOP’s agenda. As they look to the 2028 race for the White House, speculation is swirling around figures like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and former Vice President Kamala Harris as possible candidates.

articles.title: Pence blasts Huang’s Nvidia return over China chip scandal: ‘Should’ve stayed gone’
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence on Tuesday ripped Nvidia’s decision to reinstate co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang despite allegations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Pence joined a growing chorus of Republicans who have been critical of Huang’s return, which came after President Trump personally intervened to lobby the AI…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence on Tuesday ripped Nvidia’s decision to reinstate co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang despite allegations of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

Pence joined a growing chorus of Republicans who have been critical of Huang’s return , which came after President Trump personally intervened to lobby the AI titan’s board to reverse its decision to part ways with the tech executive.

Pence called on Congress to investigate the chipmaker’s business dealings and impose tougher export controls on advanced semiconductors to China after Huang’s admitted affair with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed accused of illegally smuggling advanced AI chips to China.

“America must win the race to dominate AI and allegations that Nvidia engaged in the sale of our most sensitive semiconductors to companies that were transferring that technology to China is totally unacceptable and should be deeply concerning to every American,” Pence wrote on the social platform X .

“Jensen Huang had to go and should’ve stayed gone but now that the Nvidia board and the Trump administration have signed off on reinstating Huang as CEO, it is absolutely essential that Congress get to the bottom of how and why Jensen Huang and Nvidia were able to transfer our most advanced semiconductor technology to companies doing business with China,” he added.

Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned amid revelations of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, to whom Jensen Huang is not related.

Nvidia’s board said in a statement Monday it had received assurances from senior U.S. government officials that Huang’s reinstatement posed no national security risk, and the company said its investigation into Huang would continue.

Trump, who had rallied for Huang’s return, told CNBC on Monday that he had convinced the board to reinstate the tech executive. The president also said Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed the government had no evidence that Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct.

Pence on Tuesday also invoked Huang’s criticism last year of China hawks , whom the Nvidia chief accused of wearing “a badge of shame” and being unpatriotic.

“With all due respect to the many dedicated employees and investors in Nvidia, patriotism means standing up for America against the machinations of authoritarian regimes and enduring shame awaits those who put personal and business interests above the national security and economic prosperity of the United States,” Pence wrote.

Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. The House Foreign Affairs Committee is also set to conduct transcribed interviews with Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel over potential national security breaches.

Pence urged Congress not only to investigate the circumstances surrounding the scandal but also to pursue legislative changes to prevent American technology from reaching China.

articles.title: Nvidia stock surges as Jensen Huang rehired. Thank you, Trump!
articles.summary: The business of America is business.
articles.body:
Somehow, Jensen Huang returned. That was the news yesterday — we covered it live on “Rising,” with Kevin O’Leary, who got to react to the breaking news.

Whatever you think about Huang returning to Nvidia after being accused of sleeping with a Chinese spy , and the potential national security ramifications, one thing is clear: the markets were thrilled at this news. In fact, the Nvidia stock price surged 31 percent after the markets learned that Huang was coming back.

Now look, I have issues with Huang’s actions, which certainly sound like they were reckless, even if it turns out they ultimately did not put national security at risk. I also have serious reservations about President Trump intervening to back Huang — the president reportedly called into a meeting of the board and urged them to rehire Huang. Moreover, Vice President Vance apparently worked his contacts in Silicon Valley in order to help reassure tech folks that Huang coming back was the right move. Listen to this.

But setting aside those legitimate concerns, it is the case that the government caused this drama by letting it be known that Huang had had this affair — and so if it’s true that it poses no national security problems, well then, they have an obligation to clear things up.

Now I do hope Republicans and Democrats continue to monitor the situation and, by all means, conduct investigations. But as for right now, you can’t argue with the results. The markets absolutely love the idea of Huang coming back, and apparently, so do his employees .

Kinda speaks for itself, doesn’t it? The business of America is business.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: DNC holding 12 primary debates, demands pledge against dark money
articles.summary: Democrats need this competition. I’m looking forward to that first debate in June.
articles.body:
The 2028 presidential election is still two years away, but Democrats are already preparing for what could be one of the most competitive presidential primaries in a generation.

The Democratic National Committee has announced plans for 12 presidential primary debates , with the first scheduled for June 2027. It’s exciting because, unlike previous cycles, Democrats don’t have an obvious frontrunner or heir apparent.

There are, of course, some familiar names in the mix. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff are among the potential contenders.

The DNC announcement unveiled some new rules as well — one of the biggest proposed requirements is a pledge addressing dark money. Candidates would have to denounce spending on their behalf by outside groups that do not disclose their donors. That’s a big deal, since super PACs and outside spending have become a major part of most modern presidential campaigns, and wealthy interests have influenced elections without voters even knowing who’s footing the bill.

Hopefully they’ll stick to enforcing these rules. During the 2020 Democratic primary, candidates initially embraced an informal agreement to reject super PAC support, but that quickly fell apart when candidates, including ones who had criticized the practice, accepted outside assistance. So this time, the DNC appears to be trying to establish clearer expectations from the beginning.

I also like another part of this announcement: the DNC says it plans to involve content creators and influencers in the debate process. I think that’s very smart.

The way Americans consume information has fundamentally changed. Younger voters aren’t necessarily tuning in to traditional political programming or watching a two-hour debate on television. They’re getting information through podcasts, short-form videos, YouTube, TikTok and independent digital voices. In past presidential elections, Democrats have struggled to connect with younger voters; embracing influential people on those platforms could help close that gap.

But they have to do more than just invite influencers into the room. They have to actually listen to the audiences those creators reach.

The arena is going to be interesting. Newsom has built a national profile by challenging President Trump, but California’s affordability problems could become a major vulnerability. Harris has name recognition and an existing national following, but this would be her third time throwing her hat in the ring, and she would have to confront questions about her 2024 loss and whether Democrats want another run. AOC could energize progressives but have a hard time appealing to moderate voters, while Ossoff brings a younger generation of Democratic leadership and a strong political presence in a critical battleground.

The party is still trying to figure out what it stands for, who it represents and what kind of leadership can bring its coalition together. Democrats arguably haven’t had a presidential field this wide open since the early ’90s, when a relatively unknown southern governor named Bill Clinton emerged from a crowded field and went on to win the White House in 1992.

We don’t know who that person will be this time, and that’s a really good thing. I’m looking forward to that first debate in June.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Schumer slams Trump for circumventing process in picking government watchdog head
articles.summary: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Tuesday slammed President Trump for not consulting with Democrats on Capitol Hill in nominating Eric Ueland to serve a 15-year term as comptroller general and head of the Government Accountability Office (GAO). “No president should get to pick the person who polices their power,” Schumer said in a…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Tuesday slammed President Trump for not consulting with Democrats on Capitol Hill in nominating Eric Ueland to serve a 15-year term as comptroller general and head of the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

“No president should get to pick the person who polices their power,” Schumer said in a statement. “In January, Senate Democrats are committed to honoring the longstanding bipartisan process for selecting an independent Comptroller General.”

He added, “No president is above scrutiny, and no taxpayer dollar should be beyond it.”

Democrats are accusing Trump of bypassing the bipartisan, bicameral congressional committee that’s supposed to vet and recommend candidates to lead the GAO.

They say Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.) didn’t go through the bipartisan process before sending the names of candidates to head the agency to the White House.

“Chairman Rand Paul’s office requested submissions of candidates to serve as the next Comptroller General of GAO with a deadline of less than 24 hours,” Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) said earlier this month in a statement with other senior Democrats.

“This is clearly a sham to enable President Trump to appoint a handpicked nominee to lead Congress’ watchdog,” the group added.

Gene Dodaro, the eighth comptroller general of the United States, completed his term at the end of 2025, and Orice Williams Brown is now serving as acting comptroller general.

Ueland has had a long and well-regarded career in Washington, D.C., having previously been chief of staff to former Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist (R-Tenn.) and White House director of legislative affairs during Trump’s first term.

He has also served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) during the president’s second term, working closely with OMB Director Russell Vought — which has raised concerns among Democrats and some Republicans about whether Ueland would truly be an independent leader of the GAO.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is blocking Ueland’s nomination and told The Hill that while he respects the nominee’s career, he doesn’t view him as the right fit to lead the government watchdog agency.

“He has a great reputation. He is a creature of this institution and other ones,” Tillis said of Ueland. “Unfortunately, he’s going into a role that needs the utmost independence after coming out of an organization that’s one of the most hyperpartisan. … Doesn’t work. So, for his sake, he shouldn’t be doing it.”

The outgoing senator said he views Ueland as an “honorable man” but raised concerns over his tenure at the White House budget office, which has clashed with GOP senators this Congress over pocket rescissions and other issues.

Tillis said he worried Ueland would come under pressure that could tilt his findings if confirmed as comptroller general.

“He’s at the tail end of his career, and you know how this administration works. They could absolutely destroy him on the tail end,” the North Carolina Republican warned. “That makes him vulnerable to a lack of independence.”

Paul, the Homeland Security Committee chair, is expected to hold a vote on Ueland’s nomination when the Senate reconvenes after the weeklong Thanksgiving break.

Ueland is expected to have enough votes for his nomination to move out of committee and onto the floor.

Sullivan had previously said he would wait until the results were certified by the Alaska Division of Elections, which happened Monday. With…
articles.body:
Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) has conceded the Alaska Senate race to Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D) days after the race was called by major networks, including Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s polling partner.

Sullivan had previously said he would wait until the results were certified by the Alaska Division of Elections, which happened Monday. With all votes counted, Peltola defeated Sullivan by a margin of a little more than 4 points, according to DDHQ.

“Serving Alaska in the United States Senate for the past 12 years has been the honor of a lifetime, and I thank all Alaskans for that opportunity,” Sullivan said in a statement. “As I’ve always said I would, and out of respect for the people of Alaska and our democratic process, I accept the results certified by the Division of Elections.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The GOP senator did not say whether he had spoken with Peltola. His campaign did not immediately respond to questions about whether he planned to meet with his successor during the transition.

The Alaska Senate race was the subject of intense partisan fighting, election integrity accusations and even litigation after reports from The New York Times suggested that Peltola’s campaign had recruited Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a candidate with the same name as the incumbent senator, in an effort to confuse voters. The report alleged the former congresswoman’s campaign did so in conjunction with national Democrats.

Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats denied the allegations, but Republicans capitalized on the accusations in the final weeks of the campaign, accusing Democrats of cheating and election fraud.

President Trump’s Justice Department sued to block certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan lost — a suit which was dismissed by a judge just before Election Day. The chair of the House Oversight Committee even launched a probe into Peltola’s campaign. The Trump administration recently abandoned its lawsuit .

In the end, the other Sullivan’s share of the vote was less than the difference between Peltola and the incumbent senator and thus did not make a large enough impact to affect the outcome.

Peltola will now return to Congress after losing reelection to Alaska’s at-large House seat in 2024. Her victory was part of a nine-seat gain in the Senate for Democrats nationally, the largest seat gain in a single election Democrats have seen since 1958.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins also won the race for governor, a pickup for the party, while Republican Rep. Nick Begich held onto the at-large House seat .

articles.body:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt on Tuesday chided YouTube children’s creator Ms. Rachel for meeting with families and children facing deportation at a federal youth immigration court in Lower Manhattan in New York City.

“If Ms. Rachel truly cares about all children, she should visit the Angel Family kids who lost their mom or dad to an illegal alien criminal,” Leavitt wrote on the social platform X . “Or the innocent children the Trump Administration continues to rescue from human traffickers who exploited them during four years of the Democrats’ open border.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The YouTube star, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, visited the court with Rep.-elect Brad Lander (D-N.Y.) to see how the children were being treated, New York City-based WABC reported .

“I think about how that makes a child feel whether or not you are removable. … I don’t want any child to hear that word associated with them,” Accurso told the outlet.

She said one fourth grader facing deportation was reunited with his mother, but they do not have representation.

“He came and gave me this, and it says, the first thing he wants is an immigration lawyer,” she told Spectrum News , holding up a letter that the fourth-grader wrote. “And then Nikes that are blue, and a TV. And he’ll be getting all of these things from me, don’t you worry. He just stole my heart.”

Lander said the new Democratic majority in Congress “is going to stand up for these kids,” the outlet reported.

Accurso has publicly advocated for immigrant children and against Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) practice of detaining families at Texas’s Dilley Immigration Processing Center. She spoke with Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) last Thursday about how the Lone Star State will bring an end to family detention at the facility.

Hinojosa told Accurso that she was open to working with President Trump to “take care of kids and families,” adding that officials should “come together to stop hurting kids in this country and in this state.”

The YouTuber has also used her platform to speak up for Palestinian children living through what international groups have declared a humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

Some critics have accused her of spreading propaganda for Hamas, the political militant group that led the attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing more than 1,200 Israelis and leading to the subsequent military campaign in the territory that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians.

Accurso fired back at these critics in April 2025, writing on Instagram, “All children have the right to food, water, medical care and education. All children should be protected from violence.”

Mecklenburg…
articles.body:
A North Carolina prosecutor announced Tuesday his office dropped a felony charge against Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.).

The incoming lawmaker was accused of not returning a rental car in 2019 and was served a felony warrant during an October campaign event for allegedly failing to appear for a criminal summons related to the charge.

Mecklenburg County District Attorney Spencer Merriweather said his office dropped the charges after the rental car dealership and Womack reached an agreement to do so.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“In the days that followed, we were able to confirm that the victim rental corporation received a sum of money from the Defendant equal to an assessed rental cost from the day the vehicle was deemed overdue until the day it came back into the possession of the victim corporation,” a press release from his office read.

Womack’s campaign did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

A felony conviction may have prevented Womack from serving in the House, as the Ethics Committee recommends lawmakers refrain from voting if they were sentenced to two or more years in prison.

Womack unseated incumbent Rep. Tim Moore (R-N.C.) in the race to represent North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District. She was one of several Democrats to clinch surprise victories in the Tar Heel State — contributing to the nationwide blue wave that resulted in the party claiming majorities in both chambers of Congress.

She, like many other Democrats in battleground districts, capitalized on voter discontent with the rising cost of living and ran on an affordability platform . Her campaign focused on lowering prescription drug costs, fully funding rural hospitals and strengthening the Affordable Care Act.

Moore took advantage of the felony charge Womack was facing at the time, making the criminal proceedings the subject of attack ads. But she hit back, accusing the GOP opponent of exploiting an unresolved legal matter, The Charlotte Observer reported in early November.

articles.body:
President Trump warned travelers of “slow motion” air traffic on Tuesday ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday week.

“For those traveling on the roads this holiday season, as you know, we have a very antiquated system, and we’re going to rebuild it for the airports,” Trump said, speaking at the annual White House turkey pardoning ceremony.

“The air traffic control is 57 years old. That’s like some of the younger parts of it. But we’re going to be getting the money, hopefully, from Congress so we’ll be able to build it and we’ll end up with the best air traffic,” the president continued.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“It’s totally safe, but we have to go a little bit in slow motion to keep it that way,” he said.

Trump’s comments come after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for several hours earlier this month, interrupting travel for millions of Americans.

The agency has cited a router in Arkansas and a radar site in Texas as the two likely causes of the outage.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told The Hill in an interview earlier this month that the system is “absolutely safe” for travelers ahead of the holiday season.

The Transportation Security Administration said Tuesday it expects to screen nearly 18 million travelers over the Thanksgiving week.

Before Election Day this year, a Democrat had not been victorious in a race for Texas governor in more than 25 years. Democrats also hadn’t won a Senate race in the Lone Star State since 1988, the year before Talarico, 37, was born.

Democrats’ victories in states that they have historically struggled in weren’t limited to Texas, however. They also flipped GOP seats in Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Maine, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Ohio.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) earlier this month reflected on the election results in the Lone Star State and across the country, referring to the Democrats’ victory as a “blue tsunami.”

articles.title: Al Gore plans to buy Tennessee newspaper
articles.summary: Former Vice President Al Gore is set to buy his hometown newspaper in Tennessee, citing a desire to safeguard independent local journalism as he returns to the industry where he began his career. The Carthage Courier announced Monday that the family of Hershel and Geraldine Lake, which has run the newspaper for half a century,…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Al Gore is set to buy his hometown newspaper in Tennessee, citing a desire to safeguard independent local journalism as he returns to the industry where he began his career.

The Carthage Courier announced Monday that the family of Hershel and Geraldine Lake, which has run the newspaper for half a century, plans to sell the publication to Gore.

“The agreement will be finalized and ownership will formally transfer to Mr. Gore in the coming weeks,” the Carthage Courier said in a Facebook post.

The sale will keep the 113-year-old newspaper, based about an hour east of Nashville, under local ownership.

“I’m so grateful to the Lake family for their decades of leadership in supporting independent news here in Smith County,” Gore said in a statement to The Tennessean. “Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community.”

“When my hometown paper came up for sale, I saw an opportunity to help preserve the Courier as an independent voice for Carthage and Smith County,” Gore continued. “I look forward to supporting the Carthage Courier team, many of whom have served this community for decades, as they continue to provide vital information and serve this community for generations to come.”

The Courier will retain all of its current employees under Gore’s ownership, The Tennessean reported. Scott Winfree, who has worked at the newspaper for 40 years, will step down as publisher and assume a part-time role. He will be succeeded by Roger Wells, a longtime newspaper advertising executive.

The Tennessee Press Association praised the planned acquisition, highlighting the importance of community ownership as local news outlets across the country face mounting financial pressures and layoffs.

“Much of the national conversation about local news is about decline. In Tennessee, we are seeing reinvestment,” the association said in a statement. “People who know their communities are choosing to own the local newspaper because they understand its value.”

Gore worked as an investigative reporter at The Tennessean from 1971 to 1974 after serving in the Army during the Vietnam War. He later attended law school at Vanderbilt University but left before completing his degree to run for his father’s former congressional seat in 1976.

The former vice president, who served eight years under former President Clinton before narrowly losing the 2000 presidential election to former President George W. Bush, has spent much of his post-White House career advocating for action on climate change.

articles.title: DOJ apologizes to House’s top lawyer for dispute about Omar home search
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) apologized to the House’s top lawyer, Matthew Berry, for claims he sided with the Trump administration as it sought to obtain a warrant to search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home, according to new court filings. DOJ prosecutors previously stated in filings to a federal judge that Berry “refused to be…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) apologized to the House’s top lawyer, Matthew Berry, for claims he sided with the Trump administration as it sought to obtain a warrant to search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) home, according to new court filings .

DOJ prosecutors previously stated in filings to a federal judge that Berry “refused to be involved in the search,” which they believed echoed their position that certain constitutional protections didn’t apply to a lawmaker’s private residence.

Berry — a House GOP appointee since 2023 — called this assertion “categorically false” in a statement shared with The Hill’s partner, NewsNation. He explained that while emailing with a DOJ official on Oct. 11, he clarified “that the House Office of General Counsel does not represent targets of criminal investigations in criminal matters.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“I therefore explained that during the search, the target’s personal attorney should advise him or her on whether to assert privilege over materials,” he continued.

The emails showed Berry wrote that he believed it was only appropriate for a House Office of General Counsel lawyer to observe a search for the “purpose of protecting the House’s interests … but those same equities do not apply when the search is taking place on private property.”

The DOJ admitted Tuesday it misinterpreted this section of the email to assert that Berry supported its argument that would limit the scope of the Speech or Debate Clause of the Constitution — which protects members from outside scrutiny of their legislative activities — to their private homes.

It issued an apology for the “inadvertent misunderstanding” which was included in multiple filings, conceding that Berry didn’t side with its argument.

This issue arose when a federal court unsealed records on Monday related to the search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last month. The heavily redacted documents revealed federal investigators sought evidence of potential criminal violations involving Omar dating to 1980 as part of what prosecutors described as a “preindictment investigation.”

The documents also showed a conflict between U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh and federal prosecutors over whether the search violated the Speech or Debate Clause. Documents pertaining to ongoing DOJ investigations into Omar and what crimes it is investigating were allowed to remain sealed.

The lawmaker immigrated from Somalia in 1995 before becoming a naturalized citizen in 2000. She hasn’t been formally charged by federal prosecutors with a crime and has denied the allegations.

Hassan, the incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a letter…
articles.body:
Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) is demanding answers after a report alleged Vice President Vance had a connection to a major energy company that got a license to sell Venezuelan oil soon after the U.S. captured the country’s president.

Hassan, the incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a letter to the vice president that she was opening an investigation and demanded answers on why global energy giant Vitol was awarded the license.

“I write today with serious concern that you may have used your position as Vice President to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving Venezuelan oil,” Hassan wrote. “Given the significant financial interests at stake and the importance of safeguarding government decision-making against improper influence, I am seeking information about your involvement in these arrangements.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Reuters reported Nov. 11 that an executive at Vitol, a global oil company, was offered a license to sell Venezuelan oil shortly after the U.S. captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Reuters said the executive had met with Vance a week earlier, citing a person familiar, and that Vance had vouched for him in the past to Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who asked the Vitol executive about selling Venezuelan oil.

Vance and the executive denied the meeting took place, but the executive confirmed to Reuters that Vance had vouched for him in the past. The Vitol executive was a Republican donor who had supported Vance’s Senate bid in 2022 through a super PAC, according to Reuters.

The Hill reached out to Vance’s office and Vitol for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, previously asked Vitol for more information on how it received a license to sell Venezuelan oil back in January.

Hassan’s investigation is a sign of shifting political winds in Washington. As Democrats prepare to retake the majority in Congress next year, many are already listing out investigations they want to pursue, some against President Trump and his allies.

This month’s controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s quick exit and sudden return has members of both parties calling for investigations, with Democrats demanding to know what the president knew and what his role may have been.

And an executive order Trump signed over the weekend sought to block Congress from requesting certain information from White House officials, which could be challenged by Democrats as they pursue oversight and investigations.

articles.body:
Political commentator Scott Jennings encouraged Democratic Sens.-elect James Talarico (Texas) and Scott Colom (Miss.) to run for president, as speculation rises about possible 2028 candidates.

“You want Scott’s political consulting? I’ll give you some. If I were Talarico or especially the guy in Mississippi, Colom … I would just go ahead and run for president,” Jennings said during an appearance on CNN.

Both Talarico and Colom were the victors of two of the most competitive Senate races in the country in historically red-leaning states — Texas and Mississippi.

Talarico turned Texas blue in this year’s midterm elections, winning the state’s Senate race by more than 10 points, according to The Hill’s polling partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). He defeated his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, to become the first Democratic senator in the Lone Star State since 1988.

Mississippi’s heated Senate race saw Colom defeat incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by a margin of less than 1 point, according to DDHQ .

The midterm results in Texas and Mississippi were in line with Democrats’ sweeping victories nationwide , with the party taking back control of both chambers of Congress, winning competitive races in battleground states, and flipping GOP-held seats in Kansas, Maine, Ohio and South Carolina, among others.

As for the upcoming presidential bid, several names from the Democratic Party — including New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff — have been floated as potential 2028 candidates.

Jennings, however, has opened the possibilities to the newly elected class in his recent appearance on CNN.

“This guy just flipped Texas. If he were smart, he’d be in the presidential campaign right now,” he added, referring to Talarico.

“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a post on the social platform X.

“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts,” he wrote, also noting that a federal appeals court declined to block an emergency permit for controlled explosion on Monday.

The Army announced last week that it planned to detonate degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, in a matter of days, which would produce a plume with lead-containing particles in the air.

The announcement created an uproar, causing fears that people would be exposed to toxic lead both immediately and in the aftermath. The federal government has argued that doing a controlled detonation would be more favorable than risking an accidental explosion. The saga has also raised questions about why the situation is happening in the first place.

On Tuesday, officials said they will take measures aimed at mitigating the impacts of the explosion, including using a water wall to absorb the blast impact and associated pollution.

articles.title: FAA issues and lifts ground stop at Chicago’s O’Hare
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Tuesday issued a ground stop at O’Hare International Airport in Chicago — the second brief pause on flights in two days. The ground stop was placed in effect until 4:15 p.m. local time due to an equipment outage with a ​ground surveillance radar and ​tracking system. The pause in…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Tuesday issued a ground stop at O’Hare International Airport in Chicago — the second brief pause on flights in two days.

The ground stop was placed in effect until 4:15 p.m. local time due to an equipment outage with a ​ground surveillance radar and ​tracking system. The pause in flights only applies to aircraft departing from Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Green Bay and Des Moines.

The ground stop has since been lifted , but the FAA stated that flights at the airport will be delayed “while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment. The issue is specific to O’Hare, and it does not impact all flights nor affect any other airports or FAA systems.”

Departures to O’Hare were grounded Monday “due to staffing constraints at Chicago Terminal Radar Approach Control,” the FAA told NBC 5 Chicago .

Both ground stops come after the FAA issued its third-ever nationwide ground stop of all flights due to an outage that officials believe likely originated from upgrading a copper router .

This outage, followed by several more across multiple businesses and facets of the U.S. government, like the National Security Agency , have raised questions about the country’s digital infrastructure and the potential vulnerabilities due to cyberattacks.

U.S. intelligence officials, however, have largely said these incidents were not caused by cyberattacks. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton indicated that artificial intelligence could have played a role in the outages.

Clayton said last week that upgrades, including the integration of AI, may have led to recent issues.

The stops on Monday and Tuesday hit ahead of what’s expected to be a busy travel week before the Thanksgiving holiday. Travel agency AAA projected that 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights for the holiday, a decrease of 0.2 percent from last year.

The travel agency attributed this to the cost of travel, with roundtrip domestic flights having increased by 17 percent at an average of $800 per ticket.

And House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to take over as Speaker next year, called for “ironclad export control legislation.”

articles.body:
Questions mount on RFK Jr.’s plan to regain measles elimination status

A growing measles outbreak across the U.S. is highlighting concerns about the impact of vaccine hesitancy under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s leadership.

© Jose Luis Magana, Associated Press file

Pennsylvania health officials on Monday reported a ninth death this year associated with measles — the fourth death this month — in the state.

There have been a total of 1,638 measles cases and 330 hospitalizations tied to the illness in the commonwealth in 2026, according to a Monday update to the Pennsylvania Department of Health’s measles dashboard.

State health officials said in a news release the person who passed away was not v accinated against measles and resided in Centre County.

Across the country, 2026 has been the worst year for measles in over three decades, with the number of infections more than doubling that of last year. Texas, New Mexico, New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have all reported measles-related deaths.

The Pennsylvania health agency said Monday it has administered over 7,400 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 287 pop-up clinics in affected communities.

“Dozens of additional vaccine clinics are scheduled for the upcoming weeks and months, based on community interest and need,” the department said in its Monday release.

Democratic lawmakers blasted the health secretary after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status last week. Democrats have also threatened to investigate almost every aspect of Kennedy’s tenure heading the Health and Human Services Department when they take control of Congress next year.

In a social media post last week, the secretary vowed to work with state agencies to “ regain U.S. measles elimination status” — a distinction the country held for over 25 years.

“We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust,” he wrote. “We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.”

But health experts question whether Kennedy will be able to follow through on this promise and wonder what his plan will be to fight the disease he downplayed for decades .

Kennedy has sown doubt about the safety of the MMR vaccine for years, and in his role atop HHS, he pushed for significant changes to the childhood vaccination schedule. The health secretary previously linked the shot to autism , promoted alternative treatments to measles and spread misleading messages about the vaccine — saying it contains “aborted fetus debris.”

articles.summary: Fifty-three incoming House Democrats on Tuesday warned that they could skip Harvard University’s orientation for new lawmakers in solidarity with graduate student workers on strike. articles.body:
Fifty-three incoming House Democrats on Tuesday warned that they could skip Harvard University’s orientation for new lawmakers in solidarity with graduate student workers on strike.

The incoming House members wrote in a letter to Harvard’s president Alan Garber; Jacob Watts, the Harvard Kennedy School’s director of programs and events; and provost John Manning that the university must reach a contract with the graduate student and academic workers unions.

“However, as much as we would like to attend, we have been informed that to attend your event we would be required to cross a union picket line … As newly-elected Members of the 120th Congress, we were elected because of our commitments to helping working people, and we remain steadfast in our support for unions and collective bargaining,” the letter reads.

“While we appreciate the invitation to Harvard’s Institute of Politics, we will not cross a picket line,” the lawmakers said. “So long as these workers are on strike, any trip we take to Harvard would be to stand in solidarity with our striking union siblings.”

The Harvard Graduate Students Union-United Auto Workers — which represents more than 4,000 graduate and undergraduate student workers — has been on strike since late last month.

Harvard Kennedy School spokesperson Daniel Harsha told The Hill that the program allows new members to hear from Harvard faculty and outside experts on policy issues and learn about the challenges of governing.

“Our invitation was extended to all newly elected members, and we understand and respect that the decision to attend lies with each of them,” Harsha said.

Incoming Democratic lawmakers who signed the letter included Reps.-elect Frederick Haynes III (Texas), Dan Koh (Mass.), Katy Padilla Stout (Texas), Hilda Solis (Calif.), Marni von Wilpert (Calif.), Sam Forstag (Mont.), Claire Valdez (N.Y.), Darializa Avila Chevalier (N.Y.), Angela Gonzales-Torres (Calif.), Melat Kiros (Colo.), Cait Conley (N.Y.) and Chris Rabb (Pa.).

“I’ve never crossed a picket line, and I don’t intend to start,” Forstag said in a video posted to social media Tuesday, which also featured Rep.-elects Bob Brooks (D-Pa.) and Valdez. Harvard “can afford to pay people a living wage,” Forstag added.

“To all the workers at Harvard, we’ve got your back,” the Montana Democrat continued. “And to the administration at Harvard: Well, if me and so many other members of Congress are gonna be making a trip out there in December, it’s gonna be to join our brothers and sisters on the picket line until and unless you engage in good faith in contract negotiations and give those workers a fair deal.”

Koh told The Boston Globe that he has “a lot of respect for Harvard” and for the bargaining process, but that he wants to “send a clear message that I have labor’s back.”

Bargaining began in March 2025 as the union seeks higher wages and benefits, protections for workers who are not U.S. citizens and an independent process for handling harassment and discrimination complaints.

articles.title: Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department
articles.summary: The decision follows the conclusion of the 2026 midterm elections and an effort under Trump to gather state voter rolls.
articles.body:
Alaska has terminated a memorandum of understanding that granted the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) access to the state’s voter rolls.

On Monday, outgoing Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the state’s elections, announced she had notified the Justice Department that Alaska was withdrawing from the 2025 memo, effective immediately.

In a statement, Dahlstrom said her state had entered the agreement “in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners”. But she acknowledged a shift had taken place after the 2026 midterm elections.

“The circumstances have now changed,” Dahlstrom wrote. “The election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.”

The reversal comes after months of pressure from the administration of President Donald Trump for states to surrender their voter rolls to federal authorities.

Trump has argued that such information was necessary to root out fraud during the November 3 midterms.

But officials in certain states argued that the federal government was encroaching on their constitutional authority. Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections.

Experts have also called Trump’s claims of “rigged” elections unsubstantiated .

The memorandum, signed last December at the Justice Department’s behest, established terms under which federal officials could flag potentially ineligible voters on Alaska’s voter rolls.

“Since that time, the DOJ has not identiﬁed any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the state Division of Elections said.

“No voters were removed from Alaska’s voter rolls as a result of the agreement.”

The announcement came as the state certified its November 3 midterm election results , in which Democrats flipped a Senate seat and won the governor’s office.

Alaska was one of several surprise battlegrounds during the midterms.

Democrat Mary Peltola unseated two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a fiercely contested Senate race marred by allegations of a spoiler candidate recruited to sabotage the senator’s re-election bid.

Meanwhile, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the state’s governorship, ending nearly three decades of Republican control in that office.

Democrats nationwide made significant gains, flipping both chambers of Congress in the midterms.

That result was largely fuelled by voter frustration under Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in former strongholds like Texas.

Faced with drooping approval ratings in the lead-up to the election, Trump had falsely claimed that many non-citizens were registered to vote across the country.

His administration sued some 30 states as well as Washington, DC, after they declined to hand over their unredacted voter rolls for review.

Twenty-eight of those cases were ultimately dismissed in court, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, a public policy institute at New York University.

The Justice Department suffered a further setback last month when a federal judge struck down its nationwide voter-list maintenance programme, ruling that it lacked legal authority to collect and assess state registration lists. The administration has appealed the ruling.

Alaska was one of at least 16 states that complied with the administration’s demands for voter roll access.

But it was sued by voting rights advocates for surrendering voter information, in violation of the Alaska Constitution.

In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said it had directed the Justice Department to destroy Alaska’s confidential voter information in accordance with the 2025 memo — a move that could have implications for the pending lawsuit.

On Tuesday, Democratic State Senator Bill Wielechowski suggested the latest termination was timed to prevent further scrutiny from the lawsuit.

“The real reason they did this is to try to make the lawsuit over this release go away before the incoming Gov. Kreiss-Tomkins Administration could settle or produce discovery,” Wielechowski wrote on social media.

Kreiss-Tomkins is set to be sworn in as governor on December 7.

Wielechowski also noted that Alaska’s request for the Trump administration to delete the records is “likely meaningless”, since federal authorities have “undoubtedly already loaded it” onto government databases.

In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said its decision to end the memo did not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.

The state’s interests, it added, were “best served by terminating the agreement and continuing to rely on its established voter list-maintenance procedures”.

A Justice Department spokesperson told The Associated Press on Tuesday that the department would issue a formal response to the state.
